Technology project governance is commensurate with risk and complexity: oversight roles, authority and reporting structures, and risk assessments throughout the project life cycle
Changes to source code of critical systems undergo source code review for security and recognised coding practices before introduction
System changes are independently reviewed and approved; contingency plans for unsuccessful material changes are established and tested

Contracts for critical systems developed or maintained by third parties require sufficient notice of impacting changes, demonstrated secure-by-design development, and continued accessibility of source code for business continuity
Decommissioning of critical systems minimises customer and business impact, with contingency plans established and tested for unsuccessful decommissioning
Robust policies identify and reduce shadow IT risks

No system or digital service runs with known security vulnerabilities, on outdated platforms or end-of-life technology: a current security hardening baseline, timely patching, remedial plans for approaching EOL, and management-approved, risk-assessed, annually reviewed exceptions with phase-out timelines

A patch and EOL management framework covers asset identification and risk assessment, deployment criteria, priority and turnaround by severity, compatibility testing, an end-to-end approval, testing, monitoring and tracking workflow, and end-user awareness

The effectiveness and security of technology in use is monitored against disruptive developments (e.g. quantum computing): board advice on impact, a long-term strategy with competent resources, and a migration roadmap

Project risk assessments address resource adequacy including vendors and concurrent projects, system complexity and integration, security controls through the life cycle, completeness of user requirements, robustness of testing, deployment and fallback strategies, and disaster recovery readiness

A cryptography policy requires industry-standard algorithms, message authentication, hashes, signatures and random number generation; secure key life-cycle management; at least annual review of standards and algorithms for critical and customer-facing systems; an asset inventory of cryptographic tools and algorithms with rationale and mappings; and tested compromise-recovery plans

Cryptographic controls are evaluated with due diligence; the institution retains ownership and control of encryption keys (or with an independent custodian) except for non-critical systems without customer information, manages externally generated keys to industry standards, weighs reliance on third-party assessments against risk appetite, and considers resource impact and reduced traffic visibility

Cryptographic protocols for secret and public keys follow recognised international standards and are tested; secret and private key storage and computation occur in a protected environment (HSM, TEE or equivalent) commensurate with risk

Public keys are stored in certificates from a Certificate Authority (recognised CAs for customers); authentication and signature protocols protect private keys so their use is legally binding; issuance and renewal follow industry and legal specifications
Resilience and availability objectives of data centres are specified to support business recovery objectives
Data centres have redundant capacity components and multiple distribution paths with no single point of failure

Critical systems are hosted in dedicated, physically secured production data centre space not in a disaster-prone area, with no single point of failure in hardware, electrical, thermal and infrastructure design, and with adequate maintenance and continuous monitoring with timely alerts
Data centre operations have control procedures including automated batch management, production change procedures, error handling and exception management
Incompatible activities in data centre operations are segregated (development from operations); necessary vendor or programmer access to production is authorised and monitored
System capacity is planned and managed for peak periods, growth plans and architecture changes
The board and senior management receive and review timely reports on significant project risks throughout implementation
Real-time monitoring tracks capacity utilisation and performance of key processes and services with actionable alerts; scope, metrics and thresholds are updated periodically

Key digital services and delivery channels are made resilient: early-warning mechanisms by 30 September 2027 (detect failed transactions and measure availability, monitor affected customers and volumes, escalate immediately when 5% or more of expected daily customers or transactions are affected), regular reviews of vulnerable interdependencies, and stand-in processing arrangements by 30 September 2027 prioritised for the least substitutable channels with customers informed of terms, risks and responsibilities

Critical systems with an expectation of immediate customer or counterparty service are designed for high availability: cumulative unplanned downtime at the customer interface of not more than 4 hours on a rolling 12 months and a maximum tolerable downtime of 120 minutes per incident
Diversity in technology is prioritised so critical systems infrastructure is not excessively exposed to similar technology risks

During digital service interruptions the institution escalates and decides promptly to resume via alternatives within the 10.32 timeframe, defines accountabilities and third-party arrangements for degradation, runs a communication plan with immediate customer notice, feedback handling, frequent updates and alternatives, offers a convenient availability-status check (e.g. real-time status on the website), and discloses its quarterly availability track record within 15 calendar days of quarter-end from 15 October 2027
A reliable, scalable and secure enterprise network supports business activities and growth plans
Network services for critical systems are reliable with no single point of failure against network faults and cyber threats
Real-time bandwidth monitoring and network resilience metrics flag over-utilisation and disruptions from congestion and faults, including traffic analysis for trends and anomalies

An enterprise technology architecture framework gives a comprehensive view of technology and baseline components, a technical design showing infrastructure, interconnectivity, dependencies and security controls (to find single points of failure), mappings to business functions, units, applications and data, principles for network and security design, and longer-term priorities
Network services supporting critical systems ensure confidentiality, integrity and availability of data
A maintained network design blueprint identifies all internal and external interfaces and connectivity, physical and logical, with segmentation
Sufficient network device logs are retained for investigation and forensics for at least three years
Safeguards (e.g. logical network segmentation from other group entities) minimise the risk of a compromise in one entity affecting others in the group

A backup strategy and procedures manage the backup life cycle, keep adequate copies of critical data, OS, programs, utilities, master and transaction files and event logs, store media in an environmentally secure access-controlled site, secure removable media per Appendix 1, test restoration periodically with prompt root-cause remediation, and have an independent risk assessment of end-to-end backup storage and delivery
A tamper-proof backup arrangement and an isolated recovery environment enable resumption of critical banking and payment services within tolerance after destructive cyber attacks such as ransomware
The board and senior management exercise effective oversight of third-party service providers for critical technology functions; the institution remains accountable for all resulting risks

A roadmap achieves continuous monitoring of third-party cybersecurity posture: measuring the infrastructure footprint and customer information accessible to third parties, leading product-specific controls, incident response protocols with providers for software-update vulnerabilities, a priority set of controls with frequent assurance assertions, higher-frequency monitoring of disclosed incidents, automated metric testing, and response to breached thresholds

An SDLC methodology covers requirement, design, development, testing, deployment, change management, maintenance and decommissioning, integrated with enterprise architecture, risk management and security principles including segregation of duties

A comprehensive risk assessment precedes cloud adoption, addressing deployment model sophistication, migration, infrastructure location and geopolitical and legal risk, multi-tenancy and data co-mingling, lock-in and portability, security configurability, exposure via the provider, termination and data recovery, demarcation of responsibilities and liability, and continuing regulatory and standards compliance

Customer, counterparty and proprietary data on cloud services are safeguarded against unauthorised disclosure and access, with ownership, control and management of all such data and services retained, including cryptographic key management
An access control policy governs identification, authentication and authorisation of all users to IT assets and data, with granularity commensurate with unauthorised-access risk

Access control adheres to deny-all by default, least privilege on a need-to-have basis, time-bound access, segregation of incompatible functions (development vs operations, security vs system administration, network operation vs network security, IT operations), dual-authorisation criteria, and authentication by criticality: stronger for critical activities and remote access, robust identity verification at provisioning, and credentials uniquely linked to one user

A user access matrix outlines access rights, roles or profiles and the authorising and approving authorities, reviewed and updated periodically

Access controls to enterprise-wide systems are managed and monitored, anomalies are flagged for prompt investigation, and user activities in critical systems are logged, retained at least three years and reviewed in a timely manner

Rapid development (DevOps) meets enterprise security, governance and compliance requirements, with automated IT security compliance review and automated vulnerability discovery and testing before release

Rigorous system testing precedes deployment, verifying user requirements and robustness; sensitive test data requires authorisation and disclosure safeguards

An IT operations manual documents operator tasks, job scheduling and execution, and on-site and off-site backup of data and software (frequency, scope, retention) for production and development
A problem management system responds to IT operational incidents, escalates to IT management, and records, analyses and tracks incidents to rectification; a helpdesk provides front-line support
Application performance is continuously monitored with timely exception reporting and forecasting to identify problems early and feed capacity planning
Capacity planning covers backup systems and related facilities as well as production
IT facilities and equipment are maintained per industry practice and supplier intervals, with fault and maintenance records and a hardware and facility inventory of purchased and leased assets
An IT disaster recovery plan ensures critical application systems and technology services resume per business recovery requirements (TM-G-2), with adequate insurance of IT resources
Network management responsibility is assigned to skilled, resourced individuals; network standards, design, diagrams and procedures are documented, current, communicated and reviewed periodically
Critical communications facilities are identified and single points of failure minimised by automatic re-routing, multiple exchanges and alternate telecommunications providers

Powerful network analysis and monitoring tools are protected from unauthorised use and restricted to authorised staff under approval and review
Procedures for use of networks and network services define available services, authorisation of who may access them, and protection of access points, connections and services

Internal networks are segregated by access-control need; production systems sit in dedicated segments separated from internet, extranet and market-data traffic; sensitive inter-segment traffic is controlled and tamper-protected

Security parameter settings of routers, firewalls and network servers are reviewed regularly; audit trails of critical network devices are maintained and reviewed; operations staff are alerted in real time to potential breaches

Network certification assesses LAN/WAN additions or changes (dial ports, switches, terminal servers, gateways, routers, extranets, internet) for vulnerabilities and documents approval or required controls

WLAN policies cover approval, installation, operation and administration; a risk assessment of accessible information precedes implementation; a standard WLAN security configuration and network certification apply
Stronger encryption and mutual authentication protect wireless-to-wired traffic where needed; WLANs are segregated from the corporate network (e.g. firewalls)

Guidelines govern other major technology service providers (telecommunications, network operators): selection, approval of material exceptions and avoidance of over-reliance on a single provider for critical services
A technology and cyber risk management framework proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of operations is in place, consistent with IC-1 and TM-G-1
Significant cyber incidents are reported promptly to the HKMA and, where appropriate, other relevant authorities (e.g. PCPD, CSTCB) under prevailing legal and regulatory obligations

Regular Cyber Resilience Assessment Framework (C-RAF) assessments are conducted — inherent risk assessment, maturity assessment, and iCAST for medium or high inherent risk — raising cyber defence maturity to the assessed exposure
Secure Tertiary Data Backup (STDB) is adopted so critical data can be recovered if a cyber attack compromises both production and backup environments
The AI exchanges cyber threat intelligence through the Cyber Intelligence Sharing Platform (CISP) under the Cybersecurity Fortification Initiative
